nameStory: The name 'fava bean' comes from the Latin 'faba,' which simply means bean - this was one of the first beans cultivated by humans! Also called 'broad bean' for its distinctively wide, flat pods that are much broader than your typical garden bean. The scientific name Vicia faba places it in the vetch family, showing its close relationship to these wild climbing relatives.
description: Fava beans are sturdy, upright annual plants that grow 2-6 feet tall with thick, hollow stems. Unlike climbing beans, they stand on their own without support, forming bushy plants with distinctive blue-green leaves. The plants produce fragrant white flowers with dark purple or black spots, followed by large, thick, velvety green pods. Each chunky pod contains 2-8 large, flat beans that are much bigger than typical garden beans.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 2-6 oval leaflets that feel thick and waxy, with a distinctive blue-green or gray-green color unlike most other beans

idTips.label: Pods
idTips.description: Large, thick, velvety-soft pods that are distinctively broad and flat, feeling almost cushiony when gently squeezed, much wider than regular bean pods

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White flowers with dramatic dark purple or black blotches on the wings, giving them a striking spotted appearance and sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sturdy, self-supporting plants that stand upright without climbing, with thick, square-ish hollow stems that feel substantial when gently pinched

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Large, flat beans about the size of your thumbnail, much bigger and flatter than typical garden beans, with a smooth texture

habitat: In New England, fava beans are primarily found in gardens and farms rather than growing wild, as they're cultivated crops that rarely escape cultivation. When grown, they prefer cool, moist conditions and rich, well-drained soil. You might occasionally find them growing from scattered seeds near compost piles or former garden sites.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted in early spring as they tolerate cool weather. Young plants emerge with their distinctive blue-green leaves and begin developing their sturdy stems.
seasonality.summer: Plants bloom in early to mid-summer with their spotted white flowers, followed by the development of the characteristic large, velvety pods.
seasonality.fall: Pods mature and dry on the plant, turning brown and papery. This is harvest time for dried beans, though young pods may have been harvested earlier in summer.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as this is an annual plant that completes its life cycle in one growing season.

funFact: Some people have a genetic condition called favism that makes eating fava beans dangerous - it can cause their red blood cells to break down! This condition is most common in people of Mediterranean descent, where fava beans have been grown for thousands of years.
confusionNotes: Fava beans are unlikely to be confused with other plants due to their distinctive broad, velvety pods and blue-green foliage. Unlike lima beans, which have flatter green pods, fava pods are much thicker and feel cushiony. The upright growth habit also distinguishes them from climbing beans.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'bean,' fava beans are actually vetches (Vicia) rather than true beans (Phaseolus). They're one of humanity's oldest crops, cultivated for over 8,000 years. In New England, they're grown as a cool-season crop and can actually improve soil by fixing nitrogen like other legumes.
compareHints: Unlike other vetches in New England, fava beans are much larger, bushier plants that don't climb or sprawl. While tufted vetch and hairy vetch have small purple flowers and thin, climbing stems, fava beans have large white spotted flowers and thick, self-supporting stems. The pods are also dramatically different - favas have large, broad, velvety pods while other vetches have small, narrow pods with tiny seeds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tufted vetch stands out from its vetch relatives by having the most densely packed, one-sided flower clusters that hang downward like purple bunches of grapes.

Among the vetches in New England, hairy vetch stands out for its distinctly fuzzy stems - tufted vetch has smooth stems, common vetch has larger individual flowers, and the smaller vetches like hairy tare have much tinier flowers and leaflets.
Common vetch stands out from its relatives by having flowers that appear singly or in pairs rather than in clusters like tufted vetch or hairy vetch.
Among New England vetches, lentil vetch is the smallest and most delicate, with the tiniest flowers and smoothest texture.

Among New England's vetches, bush vetch stands out for its short flower clusters of just 2-6 blooms, while tufted vetch has long, showy spikes of many flowers and hairy vetch has dense, cone-shaped clusters.
Hairy tare stands out from its vetch relatives primarily by size - everything about it is smaller and more delicate.
Among the vetch family in New England, large yellow vetch is unmistakable due to its bright yellow flowers - all other local vetches have purple, pink, or white blooms.
Among New England's vetches, spring vetch stands out for its diminutive size - both the flowers and overall plant are much smaller than tufted vetch or hairy vetch.
